newsitem.title: ITALY: All smiles and sums at Naples summit.
newsitem.headline: All smiles and sums at Naples summit.

text.p: The leaders of Italy and France were to meet on Thursday for a summit that was almost scrapped in anger but could now smooth Rome's bumpy route into a single European currency with a helping push from Paris.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi was scheduled to welcome French President Jacques Chirac to the southern port of Naples in the evening and join him at a state dinner at the start of what one economist has dubbed the "kiss and make up" summit.
Their formal talks, face-to-face and then with financial, foreign and other ministers present, will take place on Friday morning at the city's Bourbon Royal Palace.

The same building was to have been the venue for a summit between Chirac and Prodi's predecessor Lamberto Dini last November which the French head of state abruptly scuppered after Italy criticised France's nuclear tests.

There was a creeping feeling of history repeating itself on Tuesday when an angry Prodi threatened to scrap this week's meeting after Chirac publicly questioned Italy's fitness to join Europe's new currency from its planned start in January 1999.

The warning prompted Chirac into a hasty retreat and a declaration of "ardent hope" that Italy would ride the first wave of economic and monetary union (EMU). He also praised a tough 1997 budget drawn up by Prodi to try to ensure it does.

The Naples meeting is being watched with great interest by investors who have recently poured into the Italian lira and bonds. Some feel that Chirac will make amends for his gaffe by giving another vote of confidence to Italian EMU hopes in Naples.

An immediate concern in the equation for both Chirac and Prodi will be the question of when and at what level the lira returns to the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) it left so spectacularly during a currency crisis in September 1992.
Chirac has railed repeatedly -- including twice this week -- at the lira's subsequent devaluation of up to 40 percent, blaming its weakness for the woes of French exporters.

His spokeswoman said on Wednesday that the lira had since regained about 18 percent of its value and that France wanted its rapid return to the ERM as a step towards currency union -- but not at its present level which Paris still sees as too low.
"There is undoubtedly some catching-up to do," she said.

Prodi, whose 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) budget was being presented to parliament on Thursday, made clear in a French newspaper interview that he was in no mood to take further criticism from Chirac.
"I would let him know that the lira today is quite different from the lira to which he was referring. We must be clear and I will be.
"Jacques Chirac is a subtle enough politician to understand how important it is for France and Italy to cooperate on solid ground," Prodi told Le Figaro on Thursday.
The exchange rate sums are also taxing for Prodi because Italy's economy, and export industries, stand to lose out if the lira rejoins the ERM at too high a level.

He has been quoted recently as saying that around 1,050 to the German mark would be appropriate for re-entry, but on Thursday the currency was at around its highest level since August 1994 at 992 to the German mark.

David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns International in London, said Prodi would now have to weigh up whether playing for time and a rate of above 1,000 to the mark was worth the risk of watching the currency climb even higher.
"It's about farewell to four-digit-land and hello to the three-digit lira," Brown said.
